Data Munging

tattoo_modified <- tattoo %>%
  dplyr::select(Gender, Tattoo_Attractive) %>%
  tidyr::drop_na(c(Gender, Tattoo_Attractive )) %>%
  mutate(
    Gender = factor(Gender,
                    levels = c("F", "M"),
                    labels = c("Female", "Male")
    ),
    Tattoo_Attractive = factor(Tattoo_Attractive,
                              levels = c("Yes", "No"),
                              labels = c("Yes", "No")
    )
  )

glimpse(tattoo_modified)
Rows: 40
Columns: 2
$ Gender            <fct> Female, Male, Male, Male, Male, Male, Male, Male, Ma…
$ Tattoo_Attractive <fct> Yes, Yes, No, Yes, No, Yes, Yes, Yes, Yes, No, Yes, …

Chi Sqaure Test

contingency_table <- vcd::structable(Gender ~ Tattoo_Attractive,
  data = tattoo_modified
)
contingency_table

Tattoo_Attractive

gss_vcd_table <- vcd::structable(Gender ~ Tattoo_Attractive, data = tattoo_modified)
gss_vcd_table %>%
  vcd::mosaic(
    gp = shading_hsv, direction = "v",
    main = "Tattoo Attraction by Gender Mosaic Chart",
    legend = TRUE,
    labeling = labeling_border(

        "left",   # Right side
        "left",   # Bottom side
        "right"   # Left side
      )
    )
  )
Warning in legend(residuals, gpfun, residuals_type): All residuals are zero.

Inference

  • The chart and test results strongly suggest there is no association between gender and tattoo attraction in your dataset.

  • Statistically, the proportions of Yes/No responses for tattoo attraction are about the same for both males and females.

[1] 0
df <- 1
X_squared_observed <- 0
X_squared_critical <- qchisq(0.95, df)

mosaic::xqchisq(
  p = 0.95, df = df,
  return = c("plot"), verbose = FALSE,
  system = "gg"
) %>%
  gf_labs(
    x = "F value", title = "Critical and Observed Chi-Square Values"
  ) %>%
  gf_vline(
    xintercept = X_squared_observed,
    color = "red", linewidth = 1
  ) %>%
  gf_vline(
    xintercept = X_squared_critical,
    color = "dodgerblue",
    linewidth = 1
  ) %>%
  gf_annotate(
    x = X_squared_observed - 2.5, y = 0.15,
    geom = "label", label = "Observed\nChi-Square",
    fill = "red", alpha = 0.3
  ) %>%
  gf_annotate("curve", X_squared_observed - 2.5,
    y = 0.135, yend = 0.10,
    xend = X_squared_observed - 0.5,
    linewidth = 0.5, curvature = 0.3,
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.25, "cm"))
  ) %>%
  gf_annotate(
    # ***MODIFIED: Changed x from + 2.5 to + 1.5***
    x = X_squared_critical + 1.5, y = 0.15,
    geom = "label", label = "Critical\nChi-Square",
    fill = "lightblue"
  ) %>%
  gf_annotate("curve", X_squared_critical + 1.5,
    y = 0.135, yend = 0.10,
    xend = X_squared_critical + 0.25,
    linewidth = 0.5, curvature = -0.3,
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.25, "cm"))
  ) %>%
  gf_refine(
    scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(add = c(0, 0.01))),
    scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(add = c(3, 2)))
  )

Inference

  • The Chi-Square test was conducted to check the relationship between gender and whether people find tattoos attractive.

  • The observed frequencies (Female: 15 Yes, 5 No; Male: 15 Yes, 5 No) are same to the expected frequencies.

  • The Chi-Square value = 0, with 1 degree of freedom and a p-value = 1.0.

  • Since the p-value (1.0) is greater than 0.05. This means there is no association between gender and perception of tattoo attractiveness.

  • Both males and females responded in exactly the same way, showing no variation in opinion.

Proportion Test

tattoo_modified %>%
  group_by(Tattoo_Attractive) %>%
  count()
# A tibble: 2 × 2
# Groups:   Tattoo_Attractive [2]
  Tattoo_Attractive     n
  <fct>             <int>
1 Yes                  30
2 No                   10
tattoo_modified_clean <- tattoo_modified %>%
  drop_na(Tattoo_Attractive)
tattoo_modified_clean %>%
  count(Tattoo_Attractive)
  Tattoo_Attractive  n
1               Yes 30
2                No 10
tattoo_modified_clean %>%
  summarize(prop = mean(Tattoo_Attractive == "Yes"), n = n())
  prop  n
1 0.75 40

Inference

  • The test result confirms if this percentage is significantly above 50%.
tattoo_modified_clean %>%
  drop_na() %>%
  gf_bar(~Tattoo_Attractive, fill = ~Gender) %>%
  gf_labs(
    x = "Found tattoos attractive?",
    title = "Proportion of Students Finding Tattoos Attractive"
  )

Inference

  • Majority of them find tattoos attractive and it’s equally spread out

  • Again no association between gender and perception of tattoo attractiveness

mosaic::binom.test(~Tattoo_Attractive, data = tattoo_modified_clean, success = "Yes")

tattoo_modified_clean %>%
  drop_na() %>%
  specify(response = Tattoo_Attractive, success = "Yes") %>%
  generate(reps = 999, type = "bootstrap") %>%
  calculate(stat = "prop") %>%
  get_ci(level = 0.95)
# A tibble: 1 × 2
  lower_ci upper_ci
     <dbl>    <dbl>
1      0.6    0.875

Inference

  • A sample proportion test was conducted to determine if the proportion of students who find tattoos attractive differs significantly from 0.5 (i.e., 50%).

  • Out of 40 students, 30 (75%) said they find tattoos attractive.

  • The sample proportion (p) = 0.75.

  • The p-value obtained from the test is 0.0022, which is less than 0.05. This means that the proportion of students who find tattoos attractive is significantly different from 50%.

  • The 95% confidence interval (0.588 to 0.873) indicates that the true proportion of students who find tattoos attractive likely falls between 59% and 87%.

Conclusion

  • The Chi sqaure result is Not Statistically Significant. We Fail to Reject the Null Hypothesis.

  • However, because the sample size is small (only 40 participants), the test may not capture real-world differences. A larger sample is needed to draw stronger and more reliable conclusions.

  • For now, we can only conclude that within this limited sample, gender has no impact on tattoo attractiveness.
